deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page): Σ=(X,Σ) is an arrangement of pseudo-lines D_i in a projective plane X, and L∈Σ is one fixed line. Take a narrow Möbius band β_L around L. Its boundary L̃=∂Δ_L is a circle that double-covers L (the two 'banks'), with deck involution ι (the 'antipodism'). The complement Δ_L of the open band is a closed disc. Every other D_i meets L in one point p_i. So D_i meets ∂Δ in the two lifts of p_i, which are ι-antipodal, and D_i∩Δ is a chord d_i.

On this page Grothendieck axiomatizes the resulting 'système de cordes' (d_i)_L.
(a) Two chords meet in at most one point. That point is interior, and the chords cross there transversally. Together with the conditions that each d_i is a topological segment and ∂d_i=d_i∩∂Δ, this defines an 'admissible chord system'.
(b) 'Parallelism' (d_i=d_j or d_i∩d_j=∅) is an equivalence relation. For a class C with ν≥2 members, the 2ν endpoints split uniquely into two blocks S', S''. Each block consists of ν consecutive boundary points, and the two blocks are antipodal.

Geometric meaning: two chords are disjoint iff the pseudo-lines meet on L, since their unique common point has been cut away inside the band. A parallel class is exactly the set of lines other than L through a vertex of Σ lying on L. Transitivity holds because D_j∩L is a single point. The figure shows these vertices as dark marks on the boundary.

He asserts that these combinatorial conditions are necessary and sufficient for a chord system to arise from some (Σ,L). He also asserts that picking one representative per parallel class gives a 'strict' chord system, in which any two chords cross. Equivalently, this is a simple-at-infinity affine arrangement.

He then defines two kinds of boundary arcs.
- Generalization arcs: for a class C, the arcs of ∂Δ spanned by S' and by S''. One of the two, singled out via the antipodism, corresponds to the point of L∩S, where S=S(Σ) is the vertex set. Combinatorially, a multiple vertex on L can be 'generalized', i.e. pushed off L.
- Specialization arcs: defined from the triangles of the chord system adjacent to ∂Δ (the orange triangles in the figure). These are triangular cells of Σ with one side on L. They can be collapsed so that their opposite vertex t moves onto L.

The next page completes this. It takes sets σ of ≥2 consecutive boundary points whose lines are concurrent at a vertex t and are all the lines through t. The union of the triangles (t,s,s') is a 'specialization triangle', whose base on ∂Δ is the specialization arc. That page also introduces 'exceptional' specialization arcs.

Purpose: a combinatorial description of the arrangement relative to one line L, i.e. projective versus affine/wiring-diagram picture. This is used to describe the elementary degenerations (specializations) and deformations (generalizations) of a pseudo-line arrangement that move vertices onto or off L. It is a step toward understanding the stratified 'space' of arrangements and its local structure.
errors: No real mathematical error. A tacit point: within a parallel class the endpoint orders in S' and S'' must be reversed (nested chords), otherwise chords would cross. This is implied by (a) but not stated.

Sufficiency of the conditions (re-gluing a Möbius band using the antipodal identification of ∂Δ) is asserted without proof. It is correct and standard, but the handling of parallel classes (re-creating a multiple point on L) needs the block/antipodality condition exactly as stated.

ideas.what: Cutting the projective plane along a pseudo-line L (complement of a Möbius band is a disc) turns a projective pseudo-line arrangement into a chord system / affine arrangement in a disc whose boundary double-covers L
ideas.modern_name: affine (wiring-diagram) representation of a projective pseudoline arrangement with a line at infinity; antipodal chord diagram
ideas.usually_credited_to: Levi (1926), Ringel (1956), Goodman–Pollack (wiring diagrams, allowable sequences, 1980s)

ideas.what: Combinatorial characterization of chord systems coming from (Σ,L): pairwise at most one transversal interior crossing; disjointness is an equivalence relation; classes occupy two consecutive antipodal blocks of boundary points
ideas.modern_name: characterization of arrangements relative to a line / contraction at L (oriented matroid language: vertices on L ↔ parallel classes of the contraction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore in Goodman–Pollack / oriented matroid theory (Folkman–Lawrence 1978, Björner et al.)

ideas.what: Generalization arcs (multiple vertices on L that can be pushed off) and specialization arcs/triangles (boundary-adjacent triangular cells, or fans of triangles at a vertex t, which can be collapsed to put t on L)
ideas.modern_name: triangle flips / Ringel mutations and degenerations (weak maps) relative to a fixed line; local stratification of the space of pseudoline arrangements
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956) for mutations; Roudneff, Felsner et al. for triangles adjacent to a line; stratification of realization spaces: Mnëv, Björner–Las Vergnas–Sturmfels–White–Ziegler

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up a generalization/specialization calculus relative to a line L, with arcs on ∂Δ_L, apparently aimed at describing the specialization order (a stratified moduli/poset) of pseudo-line arrangements. The page only gives definitions; the global use of these arcs is not developed here.
missed.quote: appelés arcs de généralisation relatifs à L (et à C) ... On définit de plus les arcs de spécialisation, en considérant les triangles formés par le système de cordes, adjacents à ∂Δ
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The ingredients match known mutation/flip theory, but a systematic specialization/generalization stratification organized line-by-line could bear on the topology of spaces of (non-simple) pseudoline arrangements. That relationship is not obviously written down in this form. Modest interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: Careful but essentially standard combinatorics of pseudoline arrangements seen from a line at infinity. The specialization/generalization framing is a mildly distinctive Grothendieckian organization of known flip/degeneration moves, not a new result.
transcription_corrections: 'syst. de cordes admis' is probably 'admissible' (with 'admis' added above the line).
In (b) the endpoints are split into '2 segments de ν [sommets] consécutifs et antipodiques'. The '[] et antipodiques' in the left margin is an insertion into this phrase, not a separate line.
'(i.e. totalement paradis)' / '[?]' after 'syst. de cordes strict': the word is unclear in the image. Mathematically it must mean that every two chords cross (no parallel pairs).

'L'un de deux arcs, disons par L verticale, l'un ... bleu)' is unclear. It seems to be a parenthetical about colour-coding the two arcs in the figure; the essential content is 'l'un des deux arcs, défini par l'antipodisme, est contenu dans L∩S'.
'triangles formés par le système de cordes, adjacents à ∂Δ' is legible in the image and matches the orange triangles in the figure.
